openers.cretaceous-period: The Cretaceous is named for chalk, and more of it formed now than in any other Phanerozoic period. The seas rose in earnest, standing roughly 250 meters above today's by the Cenomanian, and an inland sea, the Eromanga, covered much of Australia. Gondwana's breakup, begun in the Jurassic, sped up and was largely finished by the period's end. Strange box-shaped bivalves called rudists built the reefs of the Tethys, while new life appeared on every front: the first raptors, sea turtles, social ants and termites, and birds with short, fused tails. The period began 143.1 million years ago, give or take 600,000 years.
openers.early-cretaceous-epoch: The Early Cretaceous begins 143.1 million years ago, with impacts on either side of the boundary: one in central Australia, another on the floor of the Barents Sea. Europe began rifting away from North America, and Australia filled with the inland Eromanga Sea. In the lagoons of southern England's Purbeck Group, insects, early mammals and dinosaur footprints were buried in great variety. Large carcharodontosaurid predators spread across the world, the first raptors appeared, and birds diversified into many forms. Smaller newcomers mattered too: orb-weaver spiders, social ants and termites, and the oldest known sea turtles.

reviews.late-jurassic-epoch: The Late Jurassic was a world of giants on new continents. As new ocean floor split East from West Gondwana, the Arctic began to open and Cimmeria docked against Laurasia, western North America rose in the Nevadan orogeny and its floodplains filled with the Morrison sauropods. Stegosaurs peaked, the first ceratopsians and eutherian mammals appeared, and in Solnhofen's still lagoons Archaeopteryx left its feathered skeleton. A cool interval set in about 150 million years ago, the Morokweng asteroid struck, and Tamu Massif erupted on the Pacific floor. The period ended not with a mass extinction but with a turnover, driven mostly by falling and rising seas.
reviews.cretaceous-period: Four big stories frame the Cretaceous. Gondwana finished breaking apart into the southern continents, birthing the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans and isolating dinosaur faunas on separate landmasses. Small, fast-recycled ocean plates made the basins shallower, so seas rose until a third of today's land lay underwater. In those warm, shallow seas, coccolithophores laid down more chalk than in any other period, the white cliffs of Dover among it. And on Tethyan shelves, rudist bivalves crowded out stony corals as the main reef builders, until they collapsed before the period's end.

jura-141.title: The Zuñi transgression begins
jura-141.text: North America's interior began to flood again, in a cycle that would outlast the dinosaurs. The Zuñi sequence, the continent's major cratonic sequence after the Absaroka, is a great package of rock laid down as seas spread over the stable core. It began in the latest Jurassic, peaked in the Late Cretaceous and ended by the Paleocene.

jura-142.title: Yinlong, the earliest ceratopsian
jura-142.text: Long before Triceratops, its family began with a small Chinese dinosaur. Ceratopsians, the horned-dinosaur line, appear in the fossil record around 161 million years ago, represented by Yinlong. These first ceratopsians belonged to the Chaoyangsauridae and lived in Late Jurassic China.

jura-144.title: Juramaia, a shrew-like start to the placental line
jura-144.text: The ancestors of whales, bats and people may have looked like a shrew. Juramaia sinensis, a small, shrew-like mammal from China dated to about 160 million years ago, is the oldest known eutherian. Eutherians are the branch of mammals that includes the placentals. Juramaia sits closer to the ancestry of placental mammals than to marsupials, so the split between the two lines had already happened by its time.

jura-145.title: New ocean floor splits East and West Gondwana
jura-145.text: Around 160 million years ago, Africa separated from Antarctica, and India would follow in the Early Cretaceous. Gondwana was splitting into two halves. East Gondwana held Antarctica, Australia, India and Madagascar; West Gondwana held Africa, Arabia and South America. New oceanic crust formed between them about 160–155 million years ago, and narrow ocean basins opened between both halves and Laurasia. East Antarctica moved south faster than Africa and South America, opening the Weddell, Riiser-Larsen, Mozambique and Somali basins. Spreading in the Weddell Sea began about 147 million years ago. Australia and Antarctica began pulling apart in the Late Jurassic. Magmatism of the Australia–India breakup, 158–136 million years ago, built the Wallaby Plateau.

jura-147.title: Vepriai, Lithuania's largest impact crater
jura-147.text: Lithuania's largest crater is 8 km across. An impact made the Vepriai crater sometime in the Middle or Late Jurassic. Its age is estimated at more than 160 ± 10 million years.

jura-148.title: The Morrison floodplains teem with giant sauropods
jura-148.text:
At the Cleveland-Lloyd quarry, dinosaurs died around a pond as a drought tightened its grip, leaving the densest known concentration of Jurassic dinosaurs. It is one window into the Morrison Formation of western North America, mostly river and floodplain deposits laid down between about 156.3 and 146.8 million years ago. The formation built up as the Sundance Sea retreated before highlands rising to the west.

The Morrison holds one of the best-known sauropod faunas anywhere, with 24 recognized species. Among them are Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Barosaurus, Camarasaurus and Diplodocus. Predators hunted them. Allosaurus, Ceratosaurus and Torvosaurus left bite marks on bones at the Mygatt-Moore Quarry. Morrison quarries about 150 million years old are dense with dinosaurs, making this one of the richest records of Jurassic life on land.

jura-150.title: Argoland: a disputed landmass off Australia
jura-150.text: Argoland may not have been a continent at all. This hypothetical landmass has been suggested to have rifted off northwestern Australia about 155 million years ago. A 2023 reconstruction treats it instead as an archipelago of microcontinental fragments, now in southwest Borneo and nearby. Its form, and where its remains lie, are still debated.

jura-152.title: Stegosaurs reach their peak
jura-152.text: Stegosaurus itself walked the Kimmeridgian floodplains of Wyoming, in the upper Morrison Formation. Its group had come a long way. Huayangosaurus, an early stegosaur, lived in China in the Bathonian, about 166 million years ago. By the Callovian–Oxfordian, much larger stegosaurs such as Tuojiangosaurus followed. Stegosaurids had their greatest radiation in the Late Jurassic, and stegosaurs and theropods diversified around 155 million years ago.

jura-151.title: The Nevadan orogeny raises the ancestral Sierra Nevada
jura-151.text: The Sierra Nevada has ancestors. From about 155 to 145 million years ago, the Nevadan orogeny built mountains along western North America's margin. It began as an Andean-type magmatic arc, a chain of volcanoes over the subducting Farallon plate. From the mid-Jurassic, the first of several massive batholiths, huge bodies of cooled magma, were emplaced in the northern Cordillera. Arc magmatism and the accretion of oceanic arcs built the ancestral Sierra Nevada and Klamath Mountains. Terranes such as the Tuolumne River and Slate Creek were added, and the Josephine Ophiolite, a slice of ocean crust, formed about 155–150 million years ago. Mountain building continued in the Cretaceous Sevier and Laramide orogenies.

jura-156.title: Eathiestrobus and the first pines
jura-156.text: A single cone from Scotland is the pine family's only certain fossil from before the Cretaceous. Eathiestrobus, from the Kimmeridgian, is the oldest unambiguous member of the family. The earliest pine trees are dated to about 153 million years ago. By the end of the Jurassic, most modern conifer groups had appeared, descended from voltzialean ancestors.

jura-158.title: Archaeopteryx and the first birds
jura-158.text:
Its feathers were already built for flight. Archaeopteryx lived around 150 million years ago in southern Germany, then a warm tropical archipelago, and has long been considered the earliest bird. The line between birds and other dinosaurs is blurry, though, and drawing it is not simple.

Birds evolved from small predatory coelurosaurian theropods of the clade Paraves. The first stem-group birds appeared in the Jurassic, several sources say the Late Jurassic. The earliest avialans, the bird branch, appear in the Middle to Late Jurassic, and Archaeopteryx represents them definitively. Its fossils carry advanced flight feathers, so feathers must have begun evolving before the Late Jurassic. Birds share a Jurassic debut with lizards, both among the living reptile groups that first appeared then.

jura-160.title: Cimmeria finally docks against Laurasia
jura-160.text: After crossing an ocean, Cimmeria finally ran aground. About 150 million years ago, it collided with Laurasia and stalled. The ocean floor behind it buckled under, forming the Tethys Trench. In Greece, the Hellenic orogeny records Late Jurassic collisions of Cimmerian crustal fragments with Eurasia.

jura-163.title: A cool interval closes the Jurassic
jura-163.text: The Jurassic ended in a chill rather than a heat wave. About 150 million years ago, the Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval began, and it lasted well into the Early Cretaceous. Within it came a marked temperature drop during the Tithonian, known as the Early Tithonian Cooling Event. The warmth of the Kimmeridgian was over.

jura-167.title: Solnhofen's lagoons preserve feathers and jellyfish
jura-167.text: A jellyfish has almost nothing to fossilize, yet Bavaria's Solnhofen limestones hold their imprints. These Tithonian rocks, about 149–148 million years old, form a Konservat-Lagerstätte, a site of exceptional soft-tissue preservation. The area was an archipelago at the edge of the Tethys, with salty lagoons whose oxygen-free bottom waters kept scavengers away. Animals and plants washed in were buried in soft carbonate mud, preserving dragonfly wings and stray feathers. Over 600 species are known, including 29 kinds of pterosaur and the famous early bird Archaeopteryx. Nearby sites of the same archipelago, such as Ettling, add fish, horseshoe crabs, beetles, crustaceans and turtles.

jura-168.title: The Arctic Ocean begins to open
jura-168.text: The Arctic Ocean is younger than the dinosaurs. As Pangaea's breakup continued across the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary, it opened the Amerasian Basin and the Arctic Ocean. The opening ran from around 148 to 70 million years ago. Volcanism of the High Arctic Large Igneous Province accompanied it.

jura-170.title: The Morokweng asteroid strikes South Africa
jura-170.text: An asteroid 5–10 km wide hit what is now South Africa's North West province about 146 million years ago, in the Tithonian. It was an L-chondrite, a common type of stony meteorite. The size of the buried crater is debated, with estimates from 75–80 km to 240 km; the latest is about 190 km. It struck several million years before the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary. An iridium layer in Tithonian rocks of Brazil's Araripe basin may be linked to it.

jura-172.title: The last Karoo eruptions flicker out
jura-172.text: The Karoo large igneous province did not end with one great blast. It faded with scattered eruptions around its edges, about 145 million years ago. They broke out in Patagonia, the Antarctic Peninsula, northern South Africa, Kerala and southeast Australia, places now spread across several continents.

jura-173.title: Tamu Massif, perhaps Earth's largest volcano, erupts
jura-173.text: A single volcano about as big as New Mexico lies on the floor of the northwest Pacific. Tamu Massif's basalt dome spans about 450 by 650 km, with slopes of at most one degree. It is the oldest and largest part of the Shatsky Rise, Earth's third-largest oceanic plateau, built by lava at the Pacific–Farallon–Izanagi triple junction. Tamu formed in one brief eruptive period of a few million years and then went extinct. It is likely the largest volcano yet found on Earth, though gaps in seismic profiles leave open whether it is one volcano or several. Its origin is debated: a mantle plume, melting at a mid-ocean ridge, or a recycled mantle slab.

jura-174.title: Extinction or turnover? The Jurassic draws to a close
jura-174.text: The end of the Jurassic was once counted among eight mass extinctions. Now it looks more like a complex turnover, with some groups rising and others declining, and sources disagree on whether it was a minor mass extinction at all. The evidence is mainly European. Sea level probably drove it, falling in the late Tithonian and rising again at the boundary. Reefs declined sharply at the close of the Jurassic, cutting the diversity of decapod crustaceans. Most life was not strongly affected, and several ichthyosaur and pliosaur lineages crossed the boundary. The boundary itself, 143.1 ± 0.6 million years ago, is the only period boundary still lacking a GSSP, an agreed reference point in the rocks.

cret-003.title: Tiny algae build the chalk of Dover's cliffs
cret-003.text: The white cliffs of Dover are made of algae. Chalk is built of coccoliths, the tiny calcite plates of coccolithophores, which thrived in Cretaceous seas. More chalk formed in the Cretaceous than in any other Phanerozoic period, and the period is named for it. Upper Cretaceous chalk forms the cliffs of Dover and similar cliffs on the Normandy coast of France. Coccolithophores and other calcareous nannoplankton kept diversifying through the Mesozoic, peaking at about 150 species in the Late Cretaceous.

cret-006.title: Rising seas drown a third of the land
cret-006.text: At its peak, the Cretaceous sea covered one-third of today's land area. Sea level rose in earnest from the early Cretaceous, and by the Cenomanian it stood roughly 250 meters above today's. Other estimates put it about 300 meters higher, in a hot, humid world without permanent ice. Part of the cause lay on the ocean floor. Many small, fast-recycled ocean plates made ocean basins shallower, pushing the water up. In North America this flooding, the Zuñi sequence, may have been driven by the Mid-Cretaceous Superplume, and it receded late in the period.

cret-013.title: Gondwana shatters into the southern continents
cret-013.text:
The breakup began near Tasmania. Gondwana had started to fragment in the Jurassic, but in the Cretaceous the pace quickened, and by the period's end the job was largely done. Pangaea completed its breakup into the present continents, though they sat in quite different positions.

South America, Antarctica and Australia rifted away from Africa, while India and Madagascar stayed joined. In the gaps, two oceans were born, the South Atlantic and the Indian. The breakup had consequences for life. As the landmasses parted, dinosaurs became strongly differentiated by landmass by the Early Cretaceous, each continent developing its own fauna.

cret-016.title: Strange bivalves called rudists build the Tethys reefs
cret-016.text: The main reef builders of the Cretaceous were not corals but clams. Rudists, box-, tube- or ring-shaped bivalves that arose in the Late Jurassic, became major reef builders of the Tethys. Their reefs may have driven scleractinian corals off many tropical shelves, including today's Caribbean and Mediterranean. Rudists had collapsed by the K–Pg extinction and vanished completely at the close of the Cretaceous.

cret-001.title: The Cretaceous begins without an agreed starting line
cret-001.text: Every other period boundary has an agreed reference point in the rocks. The base of the Cretaceous does not. The period and its first stage, the Berriasian, begin 143.1 million years ago, give or take 600,000 years. With no agreed reference section, or GSSP, the base is formally undefined. One proposed marker is the first appearance of Calpionella alpina. It was a calpionellid, one of the enigmatic planktonic protists with urn-shaped calcite shells that were briefly abundant from the latest Jurassic into the earliest Cretaceous.

cret-011.title: Raptors appear: the first dromaeosaurs
cret-011.text: Teeth that may belong to dromaeosaurs, the 'raptors', turn up in Jurassic rocks. Their bodies do not. No dromaeosaur body fossils are known until the Cretaceous, and the first dromaeosaurs are placed at the start of that period.

cret-015.title: Purbeck's lagoons hold insects, mammals and footprints
cret-015.text: Hundreds of fossil insect species come from the Purbeck Group of southern England. These beds span the latest Jurassic and earliest Cretaceous, and they hold one of the world's most diverse earliest Cretaceous faunas. They formed in a semi-arid setting of freshwater lakes, brackish water, tidal flats and lagoons. Besides insects, they preserve reptiles, early mammals from the famous 'Mammal Bed', and dinosaur footprints.

cret-002.title: Shark-toothed giants spread across the globe
cret-002.text: Big predators can cross continents when land bridges allow. In the Early Cretaceous, large carcharodontosaurids spread worldwide, reaching Africa, North America and South America. Dinosaur footprints suggest part of the route passed through Apulia in Italy, then joined to Africa by a land bridge.

cret-007.title: Early birds branch out, and enantiornithines take over
cret-007.text: Most Cretaceous birds belonged to a group with no living members: the enantiornithines. They dominated birdlife until they died out with other dinosaur groups at the end of the Mesozoic. Archaic birds had appeared in the Jurassic, and now avialans diversified into a wide variety of forms; some had short, fused pygostyle tails by the Early Cretaceous. True toothless birds arose from toothed ancestors in the Cretaceous. China's Jehol Biota holds a great diversity of birds, including the earliest advanced ones, and Las Hoyas in Spain preserves many enantiornithines.

cret-008.title: The Eromanga Sea floods inland Australia
cret-008.text: In the Early Cretaceous, Australia's dry heart lay under water. An inland sea, the Eromanga Sea, covered a large part of the continent. It was home to the giant pliosaur Kronosaurus, a short-necked marine reptile.

cret-010.title: Social ants and termites make their debut
cret-010.text: Ants and termites, the great social insects, first appeared in the Early Cretaceous. They arrived as insects diversified through the period. Stem-group ants such as Gerontoformica are preserved in Albian–Cenomanian amber from France. Many ant groups were present in the Cretaceous, but ants became dominant, with larger colonies, only much later, in the Eocene.

cret-012.title: The first sea turtles take to the oceans
cret-012.text: Sea turtles and soft-shelled turtles both make their first appearance in the Early Cretaceous. The first freshwater pelomedusid turtles followed around 135 million years ago. Turtles became highly diverse in the Cretaceous, as the warm climate favored their spread around the globe.

cret-019.title: A comet or asteroid strikes central Australia
cret-019.text: The ring of hills at Gosses Bluff, 5 km across, is only the eroded core of a much larger crater. An asteroid or comet struck central Australia about 142.5 million years ago, very close to the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary. The original rim, now worn away, was about 22 km across. Abundant shatter cones, cone-shaped fractures formed by shock, are the strongest evidence of an impact.

cret-020.title: Mjølnir: a bolide hammers the Barents Sea floor
cret-020.text: A bolide about 2 km wide hit the seafloor of what is now the Barents Sea, off Norway. It left a crater 40 km across, named Mjølnir, dated to 142.0 ± 2.6 million years ago.

cret-022.title: Orb-weaver spiders appear, spinning wheel-shaped webs
cret-022.text: The classic spider web, a wheel of spokes and spirals, goes back to the Early Cretaceous. Orb-weaver spiders, the builders of these wheel-shaped webs, appeared around 140 million years ago, as insects, their prey, were diversifying.

cret-024.title: Europe pulls away from North America
cret-024.text: Laurentian rocks ended up in north-west Europe, and Avalonian rocks were stranded in Newfoundland, because the new Atlantic did not follow the old Iapetus suture. Between 140 and 120 million years ago, Europe rifted away from North America in a second major phase of North Atlantic breakup. The opening seaway let cool water flow from the Boreal Ocean into the Tethys. About 140 million years ago, the Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift began forming, a first stage of Greenland's separation. The Bay of Biscay began opening around 126 million years ago and was complete by 85, uplifting the Armorican Massif.

cret-023.title: Volcanic plateaus rise where Gondwana split three ways
cret-023.text: Where Gondwana split into Antarctica, South America and Africa, the seafloor swelled with lava. The Southeast African large igneous province formed there from 140 to 95 million years ago. The Mozambique Ridge grew first, 140–122 million years ago, peaking about 120 million years ago above the Africa–Antarctica spreading zone. In a later pulse, 100–94 million years ago, the Agulhas Plateau formed over the Bouvet hotspot, along with the Northeast Georgia Rise and Maud Rise.
